name: Wahgi
confidence_why: Phillips (1976), a fieldworker's phonology monograph and the only work read that speaks to Wahgi stress, analyses stress as phonemic because its placement is unpredictable, and nothing contradicts him, though he himself warns that stress is often hard to tell apart from the word's tone melody, Cahill (2011) says nothing on stress, and Luzbetak (1954) could not be consulted.

catalog_quote: The Phonological Word in Wahgi is defined by a unit of stress placement, tone placement, ... and juncture characteristics. ... The subject of Wahgi stress has been the most difficult problem in the phonological analysis of Wahgi. In many words it is indistinguishable from the tonal patterns of those words, however, stress has been analyzed as being phonemic on the basis of its unpredictableness, and is divided into primary stress and secondary stress on the word level. The phonological word carries a unit of primary stress placement, and in words of more than one syllable a possible unit of secondary stress placement. Stress is distinguished by the length and loudness. ... The Wahgi language exhibits at least two degrees of stress, but because of the presence of high tone in most words it is difficult to distinguish whether one is hearing primary stress or high tone in the words in ques…

Stress is distinguished by the length and loudness.'), and p. 35 (printed 25) gives the second quote verbatim ('The Wahgi language exhibits at least two degrees of stress, but because of the presence of high tone in most words it is difficult to distinguish whether one is hearing primary stress or high tone'). PDF page = printed…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Wahgi with an empty rule and there are no existing statements; Phillips 1976 supplies the first explicit statement: phonemic, lexically unpredictable primary stress plus secondary stress, in a word-tone language. Compatible with the empty record (nothing to contradict); adds the rule, the tone caveat and the secondary-stress facts. Cahill 2011 (already held by the project in this folder from an earlier reading, not in my list) cites Phillips for Wahgi as a word-level-melody tone language with three melodies and says nothing about stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is phonemic and unpredictable: each phonological word has one primary stress whose position is lexically fixed (examples p. 32: /'kandzip/ 'star', /'kondzika/ 'forked stick', /'kandzip/ 'they saw' with initial stress versus /nge'nika/, /kon'dika/ (clan names), /pu'poa/ 'let us go' with second-syllable stress), realised by length and loudness. Wahgi is at the same time a tone language with three tonemes (high, low, rising) whose contrasts are word-level melodies ('phonemic tone is related to the phonological word', p. 36; up to three contrastive tonal patterns per word shape), and high tone 'freely varies with extra high tone on stressed syllables' (p. 36), so stress and high tone are often indistinguishable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'in words of more than one syllable a possible unit of secondary stress placement' (p. 31; examples marked with a secondary-stress tick p. 32). Stress Deletion Rule (§1.1.3.9, p. 27): 'three placements of stress cannot occur on three sequential syllables, and.. the middle syllable loses its stress'. Author notes he could not reliably separate primary from secondary stress from high tone (p. 25).
new_statements.exceptions: Syllabic nasals 'take a noncontrastive low tone, but are never stressed' (p. 31). Unstressed /u, e, i/ between two stressed syllables elide in rapid speech only (Elision Rule, p. 25). Syllable length varies non-contrastively with stress placement (p. 30). No statement of a default position; the author states placement is unpredictable.
new_statements.identity_note: Phillips 1976 describes Wahgi of the Minj sub-district (informants from the Berepka and Konumbka clans near Minj, south side of the Wahgi River, p. vii), and distinguishes Kuma vs Danga (p. 18) and Southern vs Northern dialects in the lateral inventory; Glottolog files both Phillips and Luzbetak under Middle Wahgi [wgi] = nucl1620. Luzbetak 1954 is titled for the Banz dialect of Middle Wahgi.

tone_statements.citation: Phillips, Donald J. 1976. Wahgi phonology and morphology. Pacific Linguistics B-36. Canberra: ANU. (open PDF, sealang PL archive)
tone_statements.quote: Three tonemes have been analyzed in the Wahgi language : high tone, low tone , and rising tone . ... it was found to be impossible to contrast one syllable of the word while maintaining the other syllables in a stable condition. ... each word pattern of from one to four syllables was manifested by up to three contrastive tonal patterns . Since, therefore, ... entire tonal patterns uttered over the length of the words must be contrasted, it has been concluded that phonemic tone is related to the phonological word.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 1.1.6.1 and 1.1.6.1.2 (Tonal analysis method A), pp. 35-36
tone_statements.summary: Three tonemes (high, low, rising) contrast as whole-word tonal patterns; alt. analysis B treats contours as level sequences; stress phonemic but hard to tell from high tone.

tone_statements.quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) Stress is unpredictable and is therefore phonemic. It is not written in orthography. Wahgi has three phonemic tones: High tone [´] which can occur on any syllable of the word Low tone [`] which can occur on any syllable, but is a glide in monosyllabic words. Rising tone which occurs only on monosyllabic words. ... The tone and stress are phonemic, but are not written.

tone_statements.summary: Three phonemic tones: high [´] and low [`] on any syllable (low a glide on monosyllables), rising only on monosyllables; stress unpredictable and phonemic; neither. no tone-marked examples.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between sources, since only one work with stress content could be opened. Internal caveat inside Phillips 1976 itself: he treats stress as phonemic and unpredictable but says repeatedly (pp. 25, 31) that in many words stress cannot be told apart from the word-level tone melody (high tone varies freely with extra-high on stressed syllables), so a catalog entry should carry both labels -- lexically placed primary stress and a three-toneme word-tone system -- rather than one alone; 'tone language with a stress statement' is the defensible alternative label. Luzbetak 1954 (both listed entries) could not be opened, so whether it agrees is unknown.

The held SIL OPD independently says stress is unpredictable/phonemic.
